common.noSession: There was no session to end. The cookie has been cleared anyway.
common.autopost: The form submits itself from {script}. It is a separate resource because this service sets script-src 'none' on every response and this page relaxes it to 'self' — an inline script would not run, and the button would be the only thing that worked. With scripting off, the button IS the mechanism.
saml2.relayStateNone: RelayState: the request carried none, so none is returned
saml2.signingIn.title: Signing in — SAML 2.0
saml2.signingIn.sub: saml-profiles-2.0-os section 4.1.4 — the response travels in the body of a form POST, so it is not length-limited and never appears in a URL, a log or a Referer header.
saml2.signedOut.title: Signed out — SAML 2.0
saml2.sessionEnded: The session for {username} has ended. It is the session the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC and WS-Federation sides share, so they are signed out too.
saml2.slo.nowhere: There is nowhere to send the {element}: {sp} has no samlSingleLogoutService on its application entry, saml2.defaultSingleLogoutService is empty, no metadata has been consumed for it, and this service has never seen an assertion consumer service URL for it either. A LogoutRequest carries no return address of its own — only SP metadata does.
saml2.slo.fixBefore: Consume its metadata, or set an address on
saml2.logoutResponse.title: Logout response received — SAML 2.0
saml2.logoutResponse.heading: A LogoutResponse arrived here
saml2.logoutResponse.ok: It has been logged and dropped.
saml2.logoutResponse.why: A LogoutResponse is an answer to a LogoutRequest, and this identity provider does not wait for one: its logout page fans out and reports, rather than driving a chain of redirects through every service provider in turn. Acting on this would make this service a federation gateway, which it is not.
saml2.idpLogout.count: {n, plural, one {# service provider was signed in on it} other {# service providers were signed in on it}}
saml2.idpLogout.linksNote: These are LINKS rather than an automatic fan-out, and that is deliberate. WS-Federation's wsignoutcleanup1.0 is an idempotent GET that works as a one-pixel image; a SAML LogoutRequest is a signed message that a service provider ANSWERS, and firing those into hidden frames would produce a page claiming a federation-wide logout it cannot observe.
saml2.idpLogout.none: This session had signed into no service provider through this profile, so there is nothing to log out of.
saml11.signingIn.title: Signing in — SAML 1.1
saml11.signingIn.sub: saml-profile-1.1 section 4.2, the Browser/POST profile — the assertion travels in the body of a form POST, so it is not length-limited and never appears in a URL, a log or a Referer header.
saml11.targetNone: TARGET: none was supplied, so none is returned
wsfed.signingIn.title: Signing in — WS-Federation
wsfed.signingIn.heading: Signing in to the relying party
wsfed.signingIn.sub: WS-Federation 1.2 section 13.2.2 — the token travels in a form POST, not in a redirect, so it is not length-limited and never appears in a URL, a log or a Referer header.
wsfed.wctxNone: wctx: the request carried none, so none is returned
wsfed.signedOut.title: Signed out — WS-Federation
wsfed.sessionEnded: The session for {username} has ended. It was the session the OAuth 2.0 / OIDC side shares, so that side is signed out too.
wsfed.cleanupOnly: This was a wsignoutcleanup1.0 request, so the session was dropped and no further cleanup requests were sent — an identity provider that fanned out on receipt of a cleanup would loop with whatever sent it.
wsfed.cleanupSent: Cleanup requests sent to {n, plural, one {# relying party} other {# relying parties}}
wsfed.pingNote: Each was fetched as a one-pixel image as this page loaded — front-channel logout, and the links above are the same URLs so a failed ping can be seen rather than guessed at.
wsfed.nothingToClean: This session had signed into no relying party through this profile, so there was nothing to clean up.
wsfed.returnNote: A link and not a redirect: the cleanup requests above load with this page, and a 302 would abandon them before they were sent.
federation.continueTo.title: Continue to {partner}
federation.continueTo.lead: This service is about to send you to {url} to sign in.
federation.continueTo.postsList: It will post these fields there: {fields}.
federation.continueTo.note: There is no script on this page and it does not submit itself. Five pages in this service DO auto-post, and each one argues for itself; this one does not, because you are leaving this service for a foreign identity provider and that is exactly the moment a deliberate click is worth having.
federation.signedIn.title: Signed in
federation.signedIn.heading: Signed in through {partner}
federation.signedIn.lead: This service is now signing you in as {username}. The session is {session}, and it is the SAME session every other protocol here reads — so an OAuth 2.0 authorization request, a WS-Federation sign-in or the admin console will now find you signed in.
federation.signedIn.subject: Subject the partner sent
federation.signedIn.neverCreated: NEVER created here: fedAutocreateUsers is off on this relationship, so the person must already have an entry
federation.signedIn.updated: ; its attributes are updated from this assertion
federation.signedIn.writtenOnce: ; its attributes are written only when this sign-in creates it (fedUpdateUserAttributes is off)
federation.signedIn.mappedHeading: Attributes mapped onto the directory entry
federation.signedIn.notWritten: nothing maps this name, so it was NOT written
federation.signedIn.noAttributes: The partner sent no attributes at all, so the entry carries only the username.
federation.signedIn.thrownAway: {n} attribute(s) were thrown away because nothing maps their names. That is deliberate — this directory has no schema, so an attribute written under an unrecognised name would be accepted silently and nothing would ever report that the name was wrong. Add a mapping on
federation.slo.title: Signed out
federation.slo.partnerSignedYouOut: The partner {partner} signed you out, and this service ended the session it had started for you:
federation.slo.nowhere: There is nowhere to send the partner its {element}: this relationship has no fedSloUrl. Set it to the partner's SingleLogoutService.
federation.slo.noScript: There is no script on this page. A LogoutResponse is the partner's to receive and this service sends it by the binding the relationship names (fedSloBinding).
federation.slo.partnerConfirmed: You are signed out here, and {partner} confirmed that you are signed out there too.
federation.slo.confirm.title: Sign out?
federation.slo.confirm.heading: Sign out of this service?
federation.slo.confirm.lead: {partner} asked this service to end the session it signed you in to (WS-Federation {wa}).
federation.slo.confirm.note: WS-Federation's sign-out is not signed by its specification, so any page can send one. That is why this service asks rather than acting on it: nothing ends until this button is pressed, in this browser. There is no script on this page.
federation.slo.sessionEnded: The session {partner} signed you in to has ended.
federation.slo.sentBack: You are signed out here, and {partner} has sent you back from its own sign-out.
federation.slo.frontchannelEnded: The session that partner session started here has ended.
federation.slo.frontchannelNote: {partner} loaded this page in a frame to end the session it signed you in to here.
federation.partners.heading: Federation partners
federation.partners.note: You signed in here through these identity providers, and your session there is still live. Each is a link or a form rather than an automatic redirect: this page runs no script, and leaving for a partner is a deliberate click.
